items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to formally prove that a relation on a set [MATH: X] is an equivalence relation.

Content:
Consider the relation [MATH: \sim] defined below:

Content:
> Let [MATH: x \sim y] if and only if the integers [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] have the same last digit.

Content:
Let's prove that this relation is an equivalence relation. First, we recall the definition of an equivalence relation:

Content:
> A relation [MATH: \sim] is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Let's prove each part in turn.

Content:
Now, we'll verify all three properties in turn:

Content:
Checking reflexivity:

Content:
> Reflexivity. Let [MATH: x \in \mathbb{Z}.] Then [MATH: x \sim x] since each integer has the same last digit as itself.

Content:
Checking symmetricity:

Content:
> Symmetricity. Let [MATH: x,y \in \mathbb{Z}] and [MATH: x \sim y,] meaning that [MATH: d(x)=d(y),] where [MATH: d(x)] is the last digit of integer [MATH: x.] Then, [MATH: y \sim x] since
> [MATH: d(x)=d(y)
> \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
> d(y)=d(x).]

Content:
Checking transitivity:

Content:
> Transitivity: Let [MATH: x,y,z \in \mathbb{Z},] [MATH: x \sim y,] and [MATH: y \sim z,] meaning that [MATH: d(x)=d(y)] and [MATH: d(y)=d(x).] Then,
> [MATH: d(x)=d(y)=d(z).]
> Hence, we have that [MATH: d(x)=d(z).] So, [MATH: \sim] is transitive.

Content:
Finally, since all three properties above hold, we can write the conclusion:

Content:
> Therefore, [MATH: \sim] is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, meaning it's an equivalence relation.

Content:
Now that we've figured out all the details, let's write down our formal proof.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to formally prove that a relation on a set [MATH: X] is an equivalence relation.

Content:
Consider the relation [MATH: \sim] defined below:

Content:
> Let [MATH: x \sim y] if and only if the integers [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] have the same last digit.

Content:
Let's prove that this relation is an equivalence relation. First, we recall the definition of an equivalence relation:

Content:
> A relation [MATH: \sim] is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Let's prove each part in turn.

Content:
Now, we'll verify all three properties in turn:

Content:
Checking reflexivity:

Content:
> Reflexivity. Let [MATH: x \in \mathbb{Z}.] Then [MATH: x \sim x] since each integer has the same last digit as itself.

Content:
Checking symmetricity:

Content:
> Symmetricity. Let [MATH: x,y \in \mathbb{Z}] and [MATH: x \sim y,] meaning that [MATH: d(x)=d(y),] where [MATH: d(x)] is the last digit of integer [MATH: x.] Then, [MATH: y \sim x] since
> [MATH: d(x)=d(y)
> \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
> d(y)=d(x).]

Content:
Checking transitivity:

Content:
> Transitivity: Let [MATH: x,y,z \in \mathbb{Z},] [MATH: x \sim y,] and [MATH: y \sim z,] meaning that [MATH: d(x)=d(y)] and [MATH: d(y)=d(x).] Then,
> [MATH: d(x)=d(y)=d(z).]
> Hence, we have that [MATH: d(x)=d(z).] So, [MATH: \sim] is transitive.

Content:
Finally, since all three properties above hold, we can write the conclusion:

Content:
> Therefore, [MATH: \sim] is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, meaning it's an equivalence relation.

Content:
Now that we've figured out all the details, let's write down our formal proof.
